analysis.one_liner: Caps how many hospital patients each nurse can be assigned, from one in trauma units to six in well-baby units.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote: it sat in two House committees from May 2009 until Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every US hospital to adopt staffing plans with fixed maximum patient loads per registered nurse — for example, no more than 1 patient per nurse in operating rooms and trauma units, 2 in intensive care, and 4 in medical/surgical units. Hospitals would have had to post their actual staffing levels publicly, keep records, and submit to federal audits. Nurses would have gained the right to refuse assignments that violated the ratios or that they were not trained for, with legal protection against retaliation. Medicare payments to hospitals would have been adjusted to cover the added costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, who the bill's findings say face higher injury and death rates when too few nurses are on duty, and the nurses themselves, who gain enforceable workload limits, whistleblower protections, and a say in staffing plans.

how_it_helps.text: Sets specific maximum nurse-to-patient ratios by unit type, taking effect within 2 years (4 for rural hospitals), with an emergency exception for declared emergencies only.
Requires hospitals to post actual staffing ratios publicly in each unit and keep three years of staffing records open to nurses, unions, and the public.

Lets a nurse refuse an assignment that would violate the ratios or that she is not trained for, and bans hospitals from firing, disciplining, or reporting such a nurse — with a right to sue for reinstatement, back pay, and damages.
Requires nurses' direct input into staffing plans and empowers the HHS Secretary to audit compliance and tighten ratios further if patient safety requires it.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which would have to hire substantially more nurses to meet the ratios, though Medicare payment adjustments and MedPAC review would shift much of the added cost to federal spending and taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: Hiring enough nurses to meet the ratios is expensive; the bill would offset hospitals' added Medicare-related costs through payment adjustments, meaning taxpayers would bear a share of the bill.

Fixed ratios are less flexible than acuity-based staffing — a nurse with four stable patients may need less help than one with four unstable ones — and critics of ratio mandates generally argue they can force hospitals to turn away or transfer patients when they cannot hire fast enough.
The bill would not by itself create more nurses; its own findings concede a nationwide shortage, and it only directs the Secretary to report to Congress on how to expand the nursing workforce.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety case is strong: research cited in the bill links low nurse staffing to a large share of preventable patient injuries and deaths, and California's experience showed such ratios are workable. The real costs are nurse hiring and the federal payment adjustments that cover hospitals' added expenses, plus the rigidity inherent in fixed ratios. The bill's design mitigates several objections — rural hospitals get extra time, emergencies are exempted, and ratios sit on top of an acuity-based planning process — but the workforce shortage question is left to a future report rather than solved.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees the day it was introduced, sent to a health subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on May 6, 2009, with 11 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees.
The following day it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and no further action was ever recorded.
It attracted 23 cosponsors — 22 House Democrats and 1 House Republican — but neither committee scheduled it, and it died there when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals avoided a federal mandate to hire more nurses and post staffing data publicly; patients and nurses got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Jan Schakowsky
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 23 cosponsors.

for.what_they_did: One of the 11 members who joined the bill at introduction.

against.name: Rep. Henry Waxman
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee, the first stop for the bill, never held a markup or moved it out of subcommittee.

against.name: Rep. Charles Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee also received the bill but never acted on it — though Rangel was himself an original cosponsor.

against.name: Hospital industry
against.what_they_did: The bill's mandatory nurse-hiring costs and enforcement provisions ran directly against hospital industry interests, which historically oppose federal staffing mandates.

sides.party_line_note: The cosponsor list was 22 Democrats and 1 Republican, and the bill never reached a vote, so the party split can only be seen in who signed on, not in a roll call.

industries.note: The bill would have forced hospitals to hire enough nurses to meet fixed patient-load maximums, post staffing levels publicly, and face audits — a direct cost and loss of staffing flexibility. Its interest in avoiding the mandate runs against patients' interest in safer staffing.
Nurses would gain enforceable workload limits, a formal role in staffing plans, and the right to refuse unsafe assignments without retaliation — the same protections that benefit patients.
The bill directs a federal study of LPN staffing and later minimum staffing requirements for LPNs, expanding their protected role in hospitals.
